Learning Objectives
Identify patient-specific and surgical factors that increase the risk of hip dislocation after total
hip arthroplasty.
Assess spinopelvic parameters in patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty.
Discuss the evaluation and management of hip dislocation after total hip arthroplasty.
History

History
Instability and dislocation after primary total hip arthroplasty (THA) are substantial and
important complications, with dislocation being the most common postoperative

complication within 3 months of primary implantation.1 Postoperative dislocation is the
most common reason for revision surgery, with rates ranging from 1% to 10% for
primary THA and 75% occurring posteriorly.2-6 Posterior dislocations typically result from
internal rotation and flexion-adduction of the hip. Patients report an acute onset pain
and inability to walk and present with limb shortening.6 Anterior dislocations typically
occur during walking (with a plant and pivot) or while lying in bed and rolling over.
The causes of postoperative instability are multifactorial and include various patient-
specific and surgical factors. Age, sex, surgical history, and neurologic comorbidities have
been implicated as patient-specific factors. Older age (>80 years), female sex, prior hip
surgery, and disorders affecting muscle strength or cognitive function contribute to an
increased risk for dislocation after THA.1
Leading surgical factors that affect postoperative instability include surgical approach,
component selection and positioning, impingement, and surgeon experience.7 Any
factor that increases the risk of impingement also increases the risk of dislocation.
Implant and component malpositioning are a common cause of instability after THA
because they cause component-component impingement or affect soft-tissue tension
via leg length and offset, which increases bone-bone impingement.1 Inadequate
anteversion or low inclination are common reasons for posterior instability, whereas too
much anteversion may be a cause of anterior instability. Smaller femoral head diameter
(32 mm or less) or poor head-neck ratio from the size of the trunnion may cause
impingement and may result in an increased risk of dislocation.1 Soft-tissue factors, such
as the integrity of the joint capsule, short external rotators, and gluteal muscles, and
soft-tissue tension may contribute to instability, even with appropriately selected
components. Adequate femoral offset decreases the incidence of instability by
optimizing soft-tissue tension.1
Despite various defined risk factors for dislocation, McArthur et al5 noted that 17% of
patients who sustain a dislocation have no known etiology for instability. Other studies
have suggested that because of advances in modern implants, most atraumatic
dislocations result from altered spinopelvic kinematics that may lead to a functionally
unsafe acetabular position.6,8

Radiographic Analysis

Radiographic Analysis
Imaging evaluation of an unstable THA implant should include supine AP pelvis, AP hip,
and cross-table lateral radiographs (Figure 1). Additional imaging studies to evaluate the
hip-spine relationship and the manner in which it contributes to instability have been
suggested and include standing and sitting lateral spinopelvic imaging studies (relaxed
and/or flexed-seated).9 The lumbar spine and pelvis should be evaluated in the following
manner:
Figure 1 AP pelvis (A) and cross-table lateral radiograph of a right hip (B) demonstrate
total hip arthroplasty. Note the anteversion of the acetabular component on the cross-
table lateral radiograph. (Courtesy of Jonathan M. Vigdorchik, MD, New York, NY.)
Step 1—Analyze standing lateral radiographs for spine deformity; measure the
anterior pelvic plane and pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis.
The anterior pelvic plane is measured as the plane between the two anterior
superior iliac spines (or the horizontal midpoint between the two if not
superimposed) and the pubic symphysis (Figure 2). The anterior pelvic plane may be
neutral (a vertical line) or tilted anterior/posterior compared with the coronal plane.

Figure 2 Standing lateral radiograph of a hip and spine demonstrate a normal
anterior pelvic plane (APP), which is completely vertical, similar to the functional
pelvic plane (FPP). APPt = anterior pelvic plane tilt, ASIS = anterior superior iliac
spine. (Courtesy of Jonathan M. Vigdorchik, MD, New York, NY.)
Pelvic incidence (the sagittal plane morphology of the pelvis) is calculated as the
angle between a line drawn from the center of the femoral heads to the center of
the S1 end plate and another line drawn perpendicular to the S1 end plate (Figure
3).

Figure 3 Lateral radiograph of a hip and spine demonstrates measurement of pelvic
incidence (PI), which is an angle created by a line connecting the center of the
femoral heads to the center of the S1 body and a line perpendicular to the S1 body.
This is a morphologic parameter that remains constant throughout life and is
representative of the anteroposterior width of the pelvis. (Courtesy of Jonathan M.
Vigdorchik, MD, New York, NY.)
Lumbar lordosis is calculated as the angle between a line drawn at the superior end
plate of L1 and another line drawn at the superior end plate of S1 (Figure 4).

lumbar lordosis (LL) as a Cobb angle between the top of the S1 body and the top of
the L1 vertebrae. (Courtesy of Jonathan M. Vigdorchik, MD, New York, NY.)
Pelvic incidence–lumbar lordosis mismatch is calculated by the mathematic formula
of pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis.
Step 2—Compare standing and sitting lateral radiographs side by side for spinal
stiffness via evaluation of changes in sacral slope (Figure 5).
Sacral slope is the angle between a horizontal reference line and a line parallel to
the superior end plate of S1.
Evaluate the change in sacral slope between the two positions to quantify spinal
stiffness.
A stiff spine is indicated by a delta sacral slope of less than 10°

Spinopelvic Evaluation

Spinopelvic Evaluation
Degenerative spine and hip pathology often coexist, with 3.5% of patients who undergo
THA having undergone prior spinal surgery.10-13 Patients with a stiff spine or spinal
fusion have an increased risk for instability after THA.14,15 Spinal stiffness is not only
observed in patients with fused spines; a degenerative spine also may be stiff. A stiff
degenerative spine and a fused spine can behave in a similar manner. The interplay
between the spine and pelvis is dynamic, and spinopelvic motion may have a
considerable effect on functional acetabular orientation and THA stability. THA
dislocation rates are increased in patients with a stiff spine. Bourne and Mehin16 noted a
SEND FEEDBACK

1.55% dislocation rate in patients who underwent THA without previous spinal fusion, a
2.73% dislocation rate in patents who underwent THA who had undergone prior short
spinal fusion (one to two levels), and a 4.62% dislocation rate in patients who underwent
THA who had undergone prior fusion of three or more intervertebral disk levels.
Multiple studies have confirmed the increased dislocation and revision rates in patients
with adult spinal deformity,17,18 non-instrumented spine disease,15 fixed spinopelvic
alignment,19 and previous lumbar fusion. Published dislocation rates range from 2.73%
to as high as 20%, with the reported relative risk for dislocation ranging from 1.62 to
7.14-16,18-22 Multiple studies have demonstrated that the relative risk of revision THA in
patients with spinal disease is at least 62% higher and as much as 700% higher than that
in patients without spinal disease who undergo primary THA.9,14-16,23
Patient classification is determined based on the presence of a spinal deformity and
spinal stiffness to better characterize the nature of hip-spine pathology as part of the
preoperative workup and to avoid preventable dislocations in this high-risk THA cohort.
Management of Hip Dislocation After THA

Management of Hip Dislocation After THA
Nonsurgical and surgical treatment options are available for the management of hip
dislocation after THA. Management depends on a complex array of factors, such as the
mechanism and acuity of dislocation, stability of hip range of motion, hematoma
formation, neurologic sequelae, and the risk of recurrence.6 Most dislocations in the
early postoperative period (70%) can be managed via closed reduction. In patients with a
posterior dislocation, bracing with the use of a knee immobilizer is effective.2
Surgical management is indicated in patients with chronic instability (more than two or
three dislocations) or a late dislocation (>5 years after THA), surgical management being
required after 1% of all THA procedures for recurrent instability.15 In addition, open
reduction is performed in patients in whom closed reduction fails or in whom re-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:47 PM
AAOS | Postoperative Hip Dislocation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000510
8/16

dislocation occurs days after reduction and component malalignment is observed on
radiographs.16
Surgical treatment options for postoperative instability or recurrent dislocation depend
on the cause of the dislocation. Wera et al23 described six categories/factors that lead to
dislocation and help guide management.
Type 1: acetabular malpositioning, which usually is managed via acetabular revision;
given recent updates in surgeon understanding, a workup of the hip-spine
relationship must be incorporated.20
Type 2: femoral component malpositioning, which usually is managed via femoral
revision; however, the difficulty of revision of certain noncemented components,
combined anteversion, and alterations in limb length and offset that affect soft-tissue
tension must be considered.
Type 3: abductor deficiency, which is managed via abductor reconstruction, gluteus
maximus transfer, or revision to a dual-mobility cup or constrained acetabular liner.
Type 4: impingement, which usually results from a combination of the
aforementioned causes and is multifactorial.
Type 5: late polyethylene wear, which is more common with conventional
polyethylene liners and managed via polyethylene liner exchange if the components
are in the appropriate position; the literature shows higher rates of recurrent
dislocation if isolated polyethylene exchange is performed.
Type 6: unclear etiology, which likely is linked to the hip-spine relationship and the
result of a combination of the aforementioned factors.
Typically, implants with increased constraint are used to manage or prevent recurrent
instability. A few options may be considered, such as the use of acetabular components
with elevated rims, the removal of osteophytes or other sources of impingement, the
use of larger diameter femoral heads, and the use of dual-mobility cups and constrained
liners.
Larger femoral head sizes effectively manage instability by improving physical function
and increasing range of motion. More specifically, femoral head sizes larger than 32 mm
decrease dislocation rates.24 In general, larger femoral heads increase range of motion

because of a larger head-to-neck ratio, and an increase in jump distance, or
displacement, is necessary for dislocation of the head to occur.3,24
Dual-Mobility Cups and Constrained Acetabular Liners

Dual-Mobility Cups and Constrained Acetabular Liners
Dual-mobility cups and constrained acetabular liners typically are reserved for patients
with recurrent instability in whom the failure rate of other surgical treatment options
likely would be high; they traditionally have been used in salvage procedures. Dual-
mobility cups and constrained devices are commonly used in revision procedures
because the dislocation risk is considerably higher in these procedures compared with
primary procedures. The success rate associated with constrained components has been
reported to be higher than 80% in short-term studies.2 Indications include failed
nonsurgical management (three or more dislocations), greater trochanter loss, abductor
insufficiency, neuromuscular disability, and multidirectional instability observed
intraoperatively. In addition, dual-mobility cups and constrained devices are used in
revision procedures after periprosthetic fracture and for other indications, such as
extensive acetabular and/or femoral bone loss, the presence of an internal fixation
device, and six or more prior dislocations.2
Dual-Mobility Cups

Dual-Mobility Cups
The concept of the dual-mobility cup was originally developed in France in the 1970s,
and its use has gradually become more widespread in the United States4,5 (Figure 6 and
Figure 7). The term dual mobility describes the cup of the implant that contains an
additional liner compared with a conventional implant, which functions as an additional
bearing surface.4,5 The metal shell that lines the hip socket encloses a polyethylene
plastic liner, which encases an additional metal or ceramic head (sized at 22 mm or 28

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000510

mm).6 This configuration allows for femoral head rotation within the polyethylene liner,
which articulates with the metal shell and the femoral head.6 Dual-mobility cups are
associated with markedly lower rates of dislocation compared with traditional fixed-
bearing implants because of the increased femoral head size; therefore, they are
considered a primary option for reducing instability after revision surgery.4,5 In primary
procedures, dislocation rates have been reported to range from 0% to 4.6%. This
dislocation rate decreases to zero to 1.4% at short-term follow-up after revision
procedures.3
Figure 6 A and B, Photographs show the dual-mobility component designed by
Bousquet. A 22.25-mm metal femoral head (not shown) is inserted into the polyethylene
head. (Courtesy of Serf Orthopaedic Implants, Décines-Charpieu, France.)

For dual-mobility cups, concerns exist with regard to increased wear relative to
traditional bearing and metal corrosion at the cup/modular liner junction.3 However,
with continually improving designs, short-term data have not demonstrated a
substantially increased wear rate. Intraprosthetic dislocation is another concern; it
occurs if the prosthetic head dislodges from the polyethylene liner.3
Constrained Liners

Constrained Liners
Constrained liners often are considered for management of instability because they
increase the threshold amount of force required for dislocation. Traditionally, these
implants commonly have been used to manage postoperative instability. Various
constrained designs have been manufactured; however, two designs are most popular.
One design involves the use of an external metal ring locked to the polyethylene liner,
which extends beyond the shape of a hemisphere to create a smaller inner diameter
space than the size of the prosthetic head (sized at 22 mm, 28 mm, or 32 mm).3
Mechanical expansion of the inner diameter must be employed to reduce the head of
the femur within this liner, after which the metal ring is locked in place to prevent

reexpansion.3 The second design is a tripolar design, which contains an outer
polyethylene liner that articulates with a bipolar component: a polyethylene shell with
cobalt-chromium backing, encasing the femoral head. This bipolar construct is snapped
into an acetabular shell, with the liner providing constraint. The liner contains an
embedded, reinforcing titanium locking ring that functions in combination with the outer
polyethylene liner to constrain the head.25,26
